ru: падать в обморок, упасть в обморок; валиться с ног, свалиться
separable: n/a — no object; the particle sits right after the verb.
gloss: To fall over suddenly from illness, heat, or exhaustion.
examples: A runner *keeled over* at mile twenty.
He looked like he was about to *keel over*.
Two people have *keeled over* in this heat already.

separable: separable — *key in the code*, and *key it in*; with a pronoun it must split: *key it in*, never ✗ *key in it*.
gloss: To type numbers or information into a keypad or a computer.
examples: *Key in* your four-digit code and press the pound key.
She *keyed in* the wrong apartment number twice.
He's *keying in* the last of the invoices now.
contrast: Key takes a plain -ed: keyed in, not keyd or keied.

separable: separable — *kick around a few ideas*, and *kick them around*; with a pronoun it must split: *kick it around*, never ✗ *kick around it*.
gloss: To discuss an idea casually, without deciding anything yet.
examples: We *kicked around* a few names for the podcast.
They've been *kicking* the idea *around* since March.
Let's *kick* it *around* at lunch and see what people think.

separable: n/a — no object; the particle sits right after the verb.
gloss: To relax completely and do nothing in particular.
examples: We *kicked back* on the porch with a couple of beers.
I just want to *kick back* this weekend.
He's *kicking back* in front of the TV with the game on.

ru: начинать действовать, начать действовать; включаться, включиться
separable: n/a in this sense — no object; the medicine or the rule is the subject.
gloss: To begin to take effect or start working.
examples: The painkillers *kicked in* after about twenty minutes.
Wait in the car until the heat *kicks in*.
The new rules are *kicking in* on January first.

separable: separable — *kick in twenty dollars*, and *kick it in*; it also stands alone: *everybody kicked in*.
transitivity: both — transitive (*she kicked in fifty bucks*), intransitive (*we all kicked in*)
gloss: To contribute money or effort to something shared.
examples: Everyone *kicked in* twenty dollars for the gift.
His parents *kicked in* the rest of the tuition.
If you're *kicking in*, tell Maria by Friday.

separable: separable — *kick off the campaign*, and *kick it off*; intransitive when the event itself begins: *the game kicks off at noon*.
transitivity: both — transitive (*they kicked off the season with a parade*), intransitive (*the game kicks off at seven*)
gloss: To start something, especially an event or a season.
examples: The mayor *kicked off* the campaign with a speech downtown.
The game *kicks off* at seven.
We're *kicking off* the year with a company breakfast.

separable: separable — *kick out the troublemakers*, and *kick them out*; with a pronoun it must split: *kick him out*, never ✗ *kick out him*.
gloss: To force someone to leave a place, a school, or a group.
examples: The bar *kicked out* two guys who were fighting.
He got *kicked out* of school for cheating.
They're *kicking* her *out* of the apartment at the end of the month.

separable: n/a — no object; the person you joke with follows with *with*: *kid around with the new guy*.
gloss: To joke and fool around instead of being serious.
examples: We were just *kidding around* — nobody meant it.
He *kids around* a lot, but he does good work.
They *kidded around* through the whole rehearsal.
contrast: Kid doubles the d: kidded, kidding, not kided or kiding.

separable: inseparable — the person always follows the whole phrase: *kiss up to the boss*, *kiss up to her*, never ✗ *kiss her up to*.
gloss: To flatter someone in authority in order to get something from them.
examples: He's been *kissing up to* the boss all quarter.
She *kissed up to* the coach and still didn't start.
Don't *kiss up to* them — just do the work.
contrast: Third person adds -es after the hissing ending: kisses up to.

separable: separable — *knock down the wall*, and *knock it down*; with a pronoun it must split: *knock it down*, never ✗ *knock down it*.
gloss: To deliberately destroy a building or a wall.
examples: They *knocked down* the old motel last spring.
We're *knocking* the wall *down* to open up the kitchen.
Half the block has been *knocked down* for the new stadium.
contrast: The k is silent: knock is pronounced NAHK, exactly like the start of nod.

ru: заканчивать работу, закончить работу; сваливать, свалить (с работы)
separable: n/a in this sense — no object; a time often follows: *knock off at five*.
gloss: To stop working for the day.
examples: We usually *knock off* around five.
They *knocked off* early on Friday.
I'm *knocking off* — see you tomorrow.

separable: separable — *knock off twenty dollars*, and *knock twenty dollars off*; the amount can sit on either side.
gloss: To subtract an amount from a price or a total.
examples: The dealer *knocked off* five hundred dollars.
They *knocked* ten percent *off* for paying cash.
He's *knocking* a few dollars *off* because the box is damaged.

ru: прекращать, прекратить; переставать, перестать (делать что-то раздражающее)
separable: separable, and in this sense the object is almost always *it* — *knock it off*, never ✗ *knock off it*.
gloss: To stop doing something annoying — nearly always heard as *knock it off*.
examples: *Knock it off*, you two — I'm on the phone.
He wouldn't *knock it off* until the teacher came over.
They finally *knocked* it *off* when the neighbor complained.

separable: separable — *knock out the champion*, and *knock him out*; with a pronoun it must split: *knock me out*, never ✗ *knock out me*.
gloss: To hit someone hard enough to make them lose consciousness.
examples: He *knocked out* his opponent in the second round.
That medicine *knocks* me *out* for ten hours.
She was *knocked out* cold when the branch came down.

separable: separable — *knock out the favorites*, and *knock them out*; the losing team can also sit inside: *knocked us out*.
gloss: To beat a team or a player so that they leave a competition.
examples: Spain *knocked* us *out* in the quarterfinals.
The defending champion was *knocked out* in the first round.
One more loss *knocks* them *out* of the playoffs.

ru: выводить из строя, вывести из строя; отключать, отключить
separable: separable — *knock out the power*, and *knock it out*.
gloss: To damage something so badly that it stops working.
examples: The storm *knocked out* power to forty thousand homes.
A single lightning strike can *knock* the servers *out*.
Cell service has been *knocked out* since Tuesday.

ru: делать быстро, сделать быстро; строчить, настрочить
separable: separable — *knock out a draft*, and *knock it out*.
gloss: To produce or finish something quickly, without much fuss.
examples: I'll *knock out* the slides tonight.
She *knocked* three chapters *out* over the weekend.
He's been *knocking out* two of these a day.

ru: браться за дело, взяться за дело; приниматься за работу, приняться за работу
separable: n/a — no object; the work follows with *to*: *knuckle down to the reading*.
gloss: To start working hard and seriously at something.
examples: You'll have to *knuckle down* if you want to pass.
He finally *knuckled down* two weeks before the exam.
She's *knuckling down* on the thesis this month.

separable: inseparable — what you trail follows the whole phrase: *lag behind the competition*, *lag behind them*, never ✗ *lag them behind*.
transitivity: both — transitive (*wages lagged behind inflation*), intransitive (*sales are lagging behind*)
gloss: To develop or move more slowly than others and fall back.
examples: Wages have *lagged behind* inflation for years.
He *lagged behind* the rest of the group on the climb.
Our region is *lagging behind* on broadband.
contrast: Lag doubles the g: lagged, lagging, not laged or laging.

separable: separable — *lap up the attention*, and *lap it up*; with a pronoun it must split: *lap it up*, never ✗ *lap up it*.
gloss: To enjoy praise or attention greedily, or to accept something without questioning it.
examples: He *lapped up* the applause.
The crowd is *lapping* it *up*.
They *lapped up* every word of his story.
contrast: Lap doubles the p: lapped, lapping, not laped or laping.

ru: срываться, сорваться (на ком-то); набрасываться, наброситься (с упрёками)
separable: n/a — no object; the target follows with *at*: *lash out at reporters*.
gloss: To suddenly attack someone with angry words.
examples: He *lashed out* at the reporters on the courthouse steps.
She *lashes out* when she's tired.
They've been *lashing out* at each other all week.

ru: цепляться, уцепиться (за что-то); привязываться, привязаться (к кому-то)
separable: inseparable — *latch onto an idea*, *latch onto him*, never ✗ *latch him onto*.
gloss: To seize on an idea or attach yourself to a person and not let go.
examples: The press *latched onto* one line of the speech.
He *latched onto* us at the party and stayed all night.
Kids *latch onto* whatever their friends are doing.

separable: separable — *laugh off the question*, and *laugh it off*; with a pronoun it must split: *laugh it off*, never ✗ *laugh off it*.
gloss: To treat something serious as a joke so that it seems unimportant.
examples: He *laughed off* the rumor at the press conference.
She *laughed* it *off*, but it clearly stung.
They're *laughing off* the criticism for now.
contrast: The gh is an f sound: laugh off is LAF awf.

ru: пускаться, пуститься (в рассказ, в спор); начинать с жаром, начать
separable: inseparable — *launch into a speech*, *launch into it*, never ✗ *launch it into*.
gloss: To start doing or saying something energetically and at length.
examples: He *launched into* a twenty-minute story about his car.
She *launches into* the same complaint every time.
The band *launched into* the chorus before the crowd sat down.

separable: inseparable — *leaf through a magazine*, *leaf through it*, never ✗ *leaf it through*.
gloss: To turn the pages of something quickly without reading it carefully.
examples: She *leafed through* the magazine in the waiting room.
He's *leafing through* the file now.
I *leaf through* the catalog every time it comes.
contrast: The verb is regular: he leafs through, he leafed through - not leaves or left.

separable: n/a — no object; the information is the subject: *the memo leaked out*.
gloss: To become known when it was meant to stay secret.
examples: The memo *leaked out* two days before the announcement.
Details are *leaking out* now.
If this *leaks out*, we're finished.

separable: n/a — no object; the thing that steadies is the subject.
gloss: To stop rising or falling and stay steady.
examples: Prices *leveled off* in the spring.
The plane *levels off* at thirty thousand feet.
Enrollment is *leveling off* after five years of growth.
contrast: American English keeps one l: leveled off, leveling off. British English doubles it: levelled, levelling.

ru: говорить начистоту, сказать начистоту; быть откровенным с кем-то
separable: inseparable — the person follows the whole phrase: *level with me*, never ✗ *level me with*.
gloss: To tell someone the honest truth, even when it is unwelcome.
examples: *Level with* me — how bad is it?
He finally *leveled with* his parents about the grades.
She's *leveling with* you, believe it or not.

ru: взлетать, взлететь; отрываться от земли, оторваться
separable: n/a — no object; the rocket or aircraft is the subject.
gloss: To leave the ground, said of a rocket or a helicopter.
examples: The rocket *lifted off* at 6:42 in the morning.
The helicopter is *lifting off* now.
Both launches have *lifted off* on schedule.

ru: расслабляться, расслабиться; не принимать всерьёз, перестать хмуриться
separable: n/a in this sense — no object; it is usually an appeal: *lighten up!*
gloss: To stop being so serious or so severe.
examples: *Lighten up* — it was a joke.
He *lightened up* once the deal closed.
She's *lightening up* in her old age.
contrast: Lightening up (relaxing) is not lightning, the flash in a storm - one extra e, and they sound different.

separable: separable with a body part — *limber up your shoulders*, and *limber them up*; usually it takes no object at all: *limber up before the game*.
transitivity: both — transitive (*limber up your arm*), intransitive (*the pitchers limbered up*)
gloss: To stretch so that your body moves easily before exercise.
examples: The pitchers were *limbering up* in the bullpen.
He *limbered up* for ten minutes first.
*Limber* your legs *up* before you run.

ru: выстраиваться в очередь, выстроиться; ставить в ряд, поставить в ряд
separable: separable when it takes an object — *line up the kids*, and *line them up*; intransitive when people form the line themselves: *everyone lined up at the door*.
transitivity: both — transitive (*line the chairs up*), intransitive (*fans lined up outside*)
gloss: To form a line, or to make people or things stand in one.
examples: Fans *lined up* around the block.
The teacher *lined* the kids *up* by height.
They're *lining up* outside already.
contrast: Line drops its e before -ing: lining up, not lineing up.

separable: separable — *line up a speaker*, and *line one up*; with a pronoun it must split: *line it up*, never ✗ *line up it*.
gloss: To arrange or schedule something in advance.
examples: We've *lined up* three interviews for Thursday.
He *lined* a band *up* for the party.
She's *lining up* investors for the next round.

separable: separable when it takes an object — *link up the two systems*, and *link them up*; intransitive about people meeting: *we'll link up at the hotel*.
transitivity: both — transitive (*link the databases up*), intransitive (*we linked up downtown*)
gloss: To join with someone or something, or to connect two things together.
examples: We'll *link up* at the hotel around six.
They *linked* the two databases *up* last year.
This trail *links up* with the river path.

separable: n/a — no object; the conversation follows with *on*: *listen in on their call*.
gloss: To listen to a conversation or a broadcast that you are not part of.
examples: Her little brother was *listening in* the whole time.
Thousands *listened in* to the hearing.
Don't say it out loud — someone might *listen in*.
contrast: The t is silent: listen in is LIS-uhn in.

ru: заглаживать, загладить (позор); заставить забыть о своём промахе
separable: separable — *live down the mistake*, and *live it down*; with a pronoun it must split: *live it down*, never ✗ *live down it*.
gloss: To make people forget something embarrassing that you did.
examples: He never *lived down* that speech.
She'll never *live* it *down*.
They're still *living down* last season.

separable: inseparable — the source follows the whole phrase: *live off his parents*, *live off them*, never ✗ *live them off*.
gloss: To get the money or food you need from a particular person or source.
examples: He's still *living off* his parents at thirty.
They *lived off* savings for a year.
You can't *live off* one paycheck in this city.

separable: inseparable — the amount or the food follows the whole phrase: *live on rice*, *live on it*, never ✗ *live it on*.
gloss: To survive on a particular amount of money or a particular food.
examples: They *lived on* beans and rice that first winter.
Nobody can *live on* twelve dollars an hour here.
He's been *living on* coffee and four hours of sleep.

ru: продолжать жить, жить дальше; сохраняться, сохраниться (в памяти)
separable: n/a in this sense — no object; the thing that survives is the subject.
gloss: To continue to exist after the person or thing that began it is gone.
examples: Her music *lives on*.
The nickname *lived on* long after he left.
Their traditions have *lived on* for three centuries.

ru: переживать, пережить; проходить через что-то, пройти
separable: inseparable — the ordeal follows the whole phrase: *live through the war*, *live through it*, never ✗ *live it through*.
gloss: To experience a hard period and survive it.
examples: My grandmother *lived through* the siege.
We've *lived through* worse than this.
Nobody wants to *live through* that again.
contrast: Live drops its e before -ing: living through, not liveing through.

separable: separable — *load up the van*, and *load it up*; it also stands alone: *we loaded up and drove off*.
transitivity: both — transitive (*load the truck up*), intransitive (*we loaded up at dawn*)
gloss: To fill a vehicle or a container with as much as it will hold.
examples: They *loaded up* the van at dawn.
*Load* the cart *up* and I'll pay.
We're *loading up* now — give us ten minutes.

separable: inseparable after *up* — *load up on snacks*, *load up on them*, never ✗ *load up snacks on*.
gloss: To get a large quantity of something to have for later.
examples: Everyone *loaded up on* bottled water before the storm.
She *loads up on* sunscreen every June.
We're *loading up on* firewood this weekend.

ru: закрывать, закрыть (на карантин, на оцепление); блокировать, заблокировать
separable: separable — *lock down the building*, and *lock it down*; with a pronoun it must split: *lock it down*, never ✗ *lock down it*.
gloss: To close a place off so that nobody can move in or out.
examples: Police *locked down* the campus for two hours.
They're *locking* the building *down* at six.
The whole city was *locked down* that spring.

separable: separable — *lock in the rate*, and *lock it in*; with a pronoun it must split: *lock it in*, never ✗ *lock in it*.
gloss: To fix a price, a rate, or an agreement so that it cannot change later.
examples: We *locked in* three percent before the rates jumped.
*Lock* that price *in* today if you can.
They're *locking in* the date this week.

ru: запирать снаружи, запереть снаружи; не впускать, не впустить
separable: separable — *lock out the workers*, and *lock them out*; with a pronoun it must split: *lock myself out*, never ✗ *lock out myself*.
gloss: To stop someone from getting in, often by accident with a key or a password.
examples: I keep *locking* myself *out*.
The company *locked out* the union for six weeks.
She's been *locked out* of her own account since Monday.

ru: запирать, запереть; закрывать на ключ, закрыть на ключ
separable: separable — *lock up the shop*, and *lock it up*; it also stands alone: *I'll lock up*.
transitivity: both — transitive (*lock the store up*), intransitive (*would you lock up?*)
gloss: To lock the doors and windows of a building when you leave.
examples: Would you *lock up* when you go?
He *locked up* the store at midnight.
She's *locking* everything *up* right now.

ru: сажать в тюрьму, посадить в тюрьму; запирать, запереть (человека)
separable: separable — *lock up the suspect*, and *lock him up*; with a pronoun it must split: *lock him up*, never ✗ *lock up him*.
gloss: To put someone in prison.
examples: They *locked* him *up* for twelve years.
This state *locks up* more people than any other.
He's been *locked up* since March.

ru: входить в систему, войти в систему; логиниться, залогиниться
separable: n/a — no object; the account follows with *to*: *log in to your email*.
gloss: To enter your name and password to get into a computer system.
examples: *Log in* with your work email.
She *logged in* from the airport.
I've been *logging in* every hour to check.
contrast: Log doubles the g: logged in, logging in. The verb is two words; the noun on the button is one - your login.

ru: выходить из системы, выйти из системы; отключаться, отключиться
separable: n/a — no object; the system follows with *of*: *log off of the network*.
gloss: To disconnect from a computer system — the same idea as *log out*.
examples: *Log off* before you leave your desk.
She *logged off* at five sharp.
He's *logging off* for the night.

ru: входить в систему, войти в систему; подключаться, подключиться
separable: n/a — no object; the site follows with *to*: *log on to the portal*.
gloss: To connect to a computer system or a website — the same idea as *log in*.
examples: *Log on* to the portal and check your balance.
Thousands of people *logged on* to watch the launch.
He's *logging on* now.

ru: выходить из системы, выйти из системы; разлогиниваться, разлогиниться
separable: separable in the transitive use, where the system does it to you — *it logged me out*; otherwise no object: *log out when you're done*.
transitivity: both — intransitive (*log out when you're done*), transitive (*the site logged me out*)
gloss: To end your session on a computer system.
examples: Don't forget to *log out* on a shared computer.
He *logged out* and shut the laptop.
The site *logs* you *out* after ten minutes.

ru: смотреть вперёд, заглядывать вперёд; планировать на будущее
separable: n/a — no object; what is coming follows with *to*: *look ahead to next year*.
gloss: To think about and plan for what is coming.
examples: *Looking ahead*, we'll need two more engineers.
The board *looked ahead* to the next fiscal year.
Nobody in this business *looks ahead* far enough.

ru: осматриваться, осмотреться; ходить по магазину, походить (без покупки)
separable: inseparable when a place follows — *look around the store*, never ✗ *look the store around*; often there is no object at all: *we're just looking around*.
transitivity: both — transitive (*look around the museum*), intransitive (*I'm just looking around*)
gloss: To walk around a place to see what is there, often without buying anything.
examples: We *looked around* the market for an hour.
I'm just *looking around*, thanks.
Have you *looked around* the neighborhood yet?

ru: оглядываться назад, оглянуться назад; вспоминать прошлое, вспомнить
separable: n/a — no object; the past follows with *on* or *at*: *look back on those years*.
gloss: To think about something that happened in the past.
examples: *Looking back*, I should have taken the job.
She *looked back* on those years as the best of her life.
He never *looks back* — that's how he stays sane.

separable: inseparable — the person follows the whole phrase: *look in on your grandmother*, *look in on her*, never ✗ *look her in on*.
gloss: To visit someone briefly to make sure they are all right.
examples: Could you *look in on* the cat while we're gone?
She *looked in on* her mother every evening.
I'm *looking in on* him after work.

ru: наблюдать со стороны; смотреть, не вмешиваясь
separable: n/a — no object; the watcher is the subject and nothing follows.
gloss: To watch something happen without joining in or helping.
examples: A crowd *looked on* while the police made the arrest.
Neighbors stood on the sidewalk *looking on*.
He *looks on* and never says a word.

separable: n/a — no object; it stands alone as a warning: *Look out!*
gloss: To be careful because there is danger — usually shouted as a warning.
examples: *Look out* — there's ice on that step!
She yelled at him to *look out*, but it was too late.
He wasn't *looking out* and walked straight into traffic.

separable: inseparable — the thing you watch for follows the whole phrase: *look out for the sign*, *look out for it*, never ✗ *look it out for*.
gloss: To keep watching so that you will notice something when it appears.
examples: *Look out for* a blue mailbox — the driveway is right after it.
We were *looking out for* your car all afternoon.
He *looked out for* her name on the list and never found it.

separable: inseparable — the person follows the whole phrase: *look out for your sister*, *look out for her*, never ✗ *look her out for*.
gloss: To take care of someone and protect their interests.
examples: Her big brother always *looked out for* her.
In that business nobody is *looking out for* you.
We *look out for* each other around here.

separable: separable — *look over the contract*, and *look it over*; with a pronoun it must split: *look it over*, never ✗ *look over it*.
gloss: To read or examine something quickly to check that it is all right.
examples: Would you *look over* my essay before I send it?
The inspector *looked* the roof *over* and found nothing.
She's *looking over* the numbers one more time.

ru: просматривать, просмотреть; перебирать, перебрать (в поисках чего-то)
separable: inseparable — *look through the files*, *look through them*, never ✗ *look them through*.
gloss: To examine a set of things one after another, usually to find something.
examples: I *looked through* the whole drawer and couldn't find the key.
He's *looking through* the applications now.
Customs *looked through* every bag on the cart.

ru: рассчитывать (на кого-то), обращаться (к кому-то за помощью)
separable: inseparable — the person follows the whole phrase: *look to your manager for approval*, *look to him*, never ✗ *look him to*.
gloss: To depend on someone for help, money, or leadership.
examples: Students *look to* her for advice.
The town *looked to* the state for emergency money.
They're *looking to* him to fix it.

ru: искать, найти (в словаре, справочнике); смотреть, посмотреть (информацию)
separable: separable — *look up the word*, and *look it up*; with a pronoun it must split: *look it up*, never ✗ *look up it*.
gloss: To find information in a dictionary, a list, or online.
examples: *Look up* the word if you don't know it.
I *looked* it *up* on my phone.
She's *looking up* the flight number now.
contrast: This is the idiom. Looking up AT the sky is just the verb look plus a direction.

ru: улучшаться, улучшиться; идти на лад, пойти на лад
separable: n/a in this sense — no object; the situation itself is the subject: *things are looking up*.
gloss: To start getting better, said of a situation.
examples: After two bad years, sales are *looking up*.
Things *looked up* once she found a job.
Everything has *looked up* since the move.

separable: separable — *look up an old friend*, and *look her up*; with a pronoun it must split: *look me up*, never ✗ *look up me*.
gloss: To find and visit someone you know when you are in their town.
examples: *Look* me *up* when you're in Chicago.
He *looked up* an old roommate while he was in town.
She's *looking up* some cousins in Ohio.

separable: separable when it takes an object — *loosen up your shoulders*, and *loosen them up*; intransitive about a person relaxing: *he loosened up after a beer*.
transitivity: both — transitive (*stretching loosens the muscles up*), intransitive (*she loosened up*)
gloss: To become less tense or less formal, or to make stiff muscles move more easily.
examples: He *loosened up* after the first round of questions.
Stretching *loosens* your hamstrings *up*.
The crowd is *loosening up* a little.

separable: n/a — no object; the particle sits right after the verb.
gloss: To have good luck, especially by chance — American English.
examples: We *lucked out* and got the last two tickets.
You really *lucked out* with that landlord.
They're *lucking out* on the weather this week.
contrast: In American English luck out means to get lucky, not to run out of luck.

ru: валить в одну кучу, свалить в одну кучу; объединять без разбора
separable: separable — *lump together the small accounts*, and *lump them together*; with a pronoun it must split: *lump us together*, never ✗ *lump together us*.
gloss: To treat different people or things as if they were all the same.
examples: Don't *lump* us all *together*.
The report *lumped together* two very different problems.
Those two styles are always *lumped together* in the press.
